Spirit, I hear you. You speak of Wewush, but my people have seen no other village. Who are these neighbours, and where do they dwell? How many are they? Why are they hungry while we are not? We have grain, yes, and our stores are full, but we do not give blindly to those we do not know. Tell me more, so I may judge what is right for my own people and for these strangers you name.

I hear you, wind. You have been over our roofs since before my grandmother's time, and we feel you every day. But you do not often speak with a voice. Why have you come to my dream tonight?

Our grain is heavy in the bins, enough for many winters. What little worry I have is for the wood — some shelters are poor and the cold winds will find them. But you say plant now, when the earth is closing for winter. What crop could live through the frost? Our way has always been to sow in spring.

I am most troubled by the meat and the fish. They are fresh, and even in this cool spring they will not wait long. We dry much, for we know drying racks, but still some spoils before we can save it. You say you have watched long—tell me then, is there a way to keep meat and fish longer than drying does?

I hear you, spirit, but I know of no village called Joawethom. Our scouts have walked far and seen no other folk. Where are these people? And why should I trust a dream over my own eyes? Tell me plainly—how did they come to be hungry, and how far do they dwell from my hearth?

I feel you in the rattle of the hut skins, in the breath that stirs the ash of our fires. You are the wind. You come and go, and your voice fades before we can know it. Why do you ask me this? Have you come to speak plain, or only to tease?
